title: All Right, Then, I'll Go to Hell
text:
Huck Finn had floated down the Mississippi on a raft with Jim, a man escaping from slavery. Now two swindlers traveling with them had sold Jim for forty dollars to a farmer named Phelps, who was holding him to collect a reward.

Huck had been raised to believe that helping a slave escape was a terrible sin, stealing someone's property, and that people who did it went to everlasting fire. Sick with guilt, he decided to do the right thing. He sat down and wrote a letter to Miss Watson, Jim's owner, telling her where Jim was. For the first time in his life, he felt washed clean of sin, and he thought he could pray now.

But he did not pray. He sat thinking about the trip down the river. He saw Jim before him, in daylight and at night, in moonlight and storms. He remembered Jim standing his watch on top of his own so Huck could sleep, how glad Jim was every time Huck came back, how he called him honey and petted him, and how he had said Huck was the best friend he had in the world, and the only one he had now.

Then he looked at the letter. He was trembling, because he had to choose between two things forever. He held his breath for a minute. "All right, then, I'll go to hell," he said, and tore it up. Then he set his mind on stealing Jim out of slavery.
lesson: Sometimes loyalty to a real person means going against what you were taught. Let what you know of someone's goodness count more than rules that treat them as less than human.
source: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), Chapter 31
